Missing data

2026-11-24

Source: vignettes/missing.Rmd
missing.Rmd

mcp allows missing values (NA) in the response. This article covers two consequences of that:

  1. Change points in voids: Change points can be inferred in regions with no observed responses.
  2. Imputing missing responses: imputed() gives you the missing responses sampled jointly with the model parameters. Use it to inspect a gap or complete your data.
library(mcp)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Inferring change points in voids

Sometimes the interest is not in recovering individual missing responses, but in how gaps in the data affect inference about the change points. To demonstrate this, mcp_example("void") takes the data from mcp_example("demo") and sets the responses near both change points to NA (25 < time < 42 and 70 < time < 80). The top panel shows the fit to the full data and the bottom panel the fit with the voids:

fit_void = mcp_example("void", sample = "both")
## NA values detected in 'response'. JAGS will treat them as latent responses and impute them during sampling.

The message confirms that mcp detected the missing responses.

Notice that mcp can infer change points in regions with no observed data. The first change point joins a plateau to a slope. Its location in the void is mostly informed by extrapolating the two segments until they meet, and the uncertainty is greater than in the full data because fewer data inform these trends. In principle, it could be known to great precision if the segments’ trends were very well defined.

The second change point is different because segment 3 is disjoined from segment 2. There is nothing in the void that tells where the jump happened, so the change point posterior is roughly uniform across the void. This is true for any gap between data: the narrow gap between two neighboring data points (top panel) also yields a uniform-like posterior, just on a much smaller range.

We can quantify how much of each change point posterior is within its void using hypothesis(). Because we sampled the prior too (sample = "both"), it also returns a Bayes factor (BF) for each interval, i.e., how much the data shifted the odds of the change point being in the void:

hypothesis(fit_void, c(
  "cp_1 > 25 & cp_1 < 42",
  "cp_2 > 70 & cp_2 < 80"
))
## # A tibble: 2 × 7
##   hypothesis             mean    sd lower upper  prob    BF
##   <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 cp_1 > 25 & cp_1 < 42    NA    NA    NA    NA 0.933  45.1
## 2 cp_2 > 70 & cp_2 < 80    NA    NA    NA    NA 0.848  30.2

Imputing missing responses

The built-in example has a change in slope, a difference between two states, and several missing responses. Use imputed() to see the mean and an 80% interval for each missing response. .row gives its row number in fit$data.

# Fits model and plots it. See code in fit$example_code.
fit = mcp_example("missing")
## NA values detected in 'y'. JAGS will treat them as latent responses and impute them during sampling.
# Get imputations
imputations = imputed(fit, width = 0.8)
imputations
## # A tibble: 10 × 8
##        y     x state  .row .mean   .sd .lower .upper
##    <dbl> <int> <fct> <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
##  1    NA     8 B         8  35.4  4.45  29.7    41.2
##  2    NA    19 A        19  15.5  4.30   9.99   21.0
##  3    NA    27 A        27  17.2  4.34  11.6    22.7
##  4    NA    28 B        28  39.4  4.30  33.9    44.7
##  5    NA    29 A        29  17.6  4.40  11.9    23.3
##  6    NA    30 B        30  39.8  4.39  34.2    45.3
##  7    NA    31 A        31  17.9  4.43  12.3    23.6
##  8    NA    68 B        68  41.2  4.45  35.6    46.9
##  9    NA    84 B        84  34.6  4.37  29.0    40.2
## 10    NA    96 B        96  29.6  4.44  23.9    35.3

Use fitted() for the expected response at each row and predict() for a fresh response. Both return all rows, so you can use filter(is.na(y)) to inspect the missing responses. For this model, predictions and imputations at the gaps have the same distribution. In a time series, they can differ, and imputed() use more available information.

Visualizing imputations

Add the imputation summaries to plot() with geom_linerange() for the interval and an × for the mean.

# Start with mcp plot with prediction interval
plot(fit, color_by = "state", interval = "predict", width = 0.8) +

  # Add imputation interval
  geom_linerange(
    data = imputations,
    aes(x = x, ymin = .lower, ymax = .upper),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "black"
  ) +

  # Add "x" at posterior mean
  geom_point(
    data = imputations,
    aes(x = x, y = .mean),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 4,  # an "x"
    size = 2
  )

Use summary = FALSE to plot the distribution of each missing response from its draws, which is richer than just the interval plotted above.

missing_draws = imputed(fit, summary = FALSE)

ggplot(missing_draws, aes(x = .imputed)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~x)

Probabilities for a missing response

To estimate the probability that the missing response at row 19 exceeded 20, calculate the fraction of its draws above 20. Similarly for other probabilities:

missing_draws |>
  filter(.row == 19) |>
  summarise(
    p_greater = mean(.imputed > 20),
    p_lower = mean(.imputed < 10),
    p_between = mean(.imputed > 10 & .imputed < 20)
  )
## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   p_greater p_lower p_between
##       <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
## 1     0.147   0.100     0.752

Completing a dataset (multiple imputation)

With complete = TRUE, .imputed contains the observed responses as well as the imputed ones. Each .draw gives one joint completion of the data. For multiple imputation, select a few draws and make one dataset per draw.

completed = imputed(fit, complete = TRUE, summary = FALSE, ndraws = 20) |>
  mutate(y = .imputed)
datasets = split(select(completed, all_of(names(fit$data))), completed$.draw)

# Show one completed dataset
datasets[1]
## $`264`
## # A tibble: 100 × 3
##        y     x state
##    <dbl> <int> <fct>
##  1  15.7     1 A    
##  2  30.2     2 B    
##  3  12.2     3 A    
##  4  35.5     4 B    
##  5  12.9     5 A    
##  6  33.1     6 B    
##  7  17.8     7 A    
##  8  29.0     8 B    
##  9  20.3     9 A    
## 10  34.2    10 B    
## # ℹ 90 more rows

Imputations in time series

Use imputed() to fill a gap in an AR/MA series. The observed responses on both sides can inform the imputation. For example, in a Gaussian AR(1) model with mean 0 and coefficient 0.8, the middle response in c(0, NA, 10) has an imputed mean of about 4.9. The fresh prediction at that row has mean 0, based on the preceding response.

Default predict() uses the history up to each row to generate a fresh response. Earlier imputations in that history can already contain information from later observations. Use predict(fit, arma = "replicate") to generate a fresh series recursively. See the time-series article for examples.

Supported models and limitations

Supported model features

Missing responses work with the usual mcp model features. For example, you can:

  • Include continuous and categorical predictors so imputations follow observed covariate information.
  • Use group-level effects so sparsely observed groups borrow information from the population and their available observations.
  • Model changing residual standard deviation with sigma() so imputation uncertainty can vary over the predictor range.
  • Use binomial, Bernoulli, Poisson, or negative-binomial responses. The imputation draws are discrete. Use imputed(fit, rate = TRUE) for binomial proportions.

However, predictors required by the model must themselves be observed. mcp currently imputes missing responses, not missing predictor values, and it does not model the process that caused responses to be missing. As with ordinary regression using incomplete outcomes, interpretation relies on the missing responses being reasonably explained by the observed predictors and model structure.

Model evaluation and time series

log_lik(), loo(), and waic() score observed responses. In AR/MA models, these functions are unavailable when a missing response enters the history of a later observed response. Scoring that observation would require integrating over the missing history.

The time-series article discusses this. Use predict(fit, arma = "replicate") or posterior_predict(fit, arma = "replicate") to generate fresh replicated series recursively.

Predictions for new data

Use predict() with newdata to generate responses at new predictor values. For the example without AR/MA terms, supply the predictor values directly.

newdata = data.frame(
  x = c(20, 80),
  state = factor(c("A", "B"), levels = levels(fit$data$state))
)

predict(fit, newdata = newdata, width = 0.8)
## # A tibble: 2 × 7
##       x state  .row .mean   .sd .lower .upper
##   <dbl> <fct> <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1    20 A         1  15.7  4.35   10.2   21.3
## 2    80 B         2  36.2  4.36   30.7   41.8
